pairs.question: Why does the vector store live in its own SQLite file instead of a table in the graph database?

gold.decision_verbatim:
The store is a SEPARATE SQLite file, <cache>/vectors/<project>.db, and
that is the decision worth arguing. A full re-index does not edit the
graph database, it RENAMES a new one over it — so a vector table living
inside it is destroyed by every successful re-index, throwing away 23.5
CPU-minutes of encoding that was still correct because the declarations
did not change. This table also scales with the corpus where nothing
else in the store does, so inside the graph file it would be scanned by
every integrity check, copied by every VACUUM INTO, and shipped to
teammates inside graph.db.zst as 17 MB of float32 they cannot use. And
the graph database is not written by SQLite at all: it comes out of a
hand-rolled B-tree page writer whose sqlite_master is hardcoded, which
is not a thing to extend for a pass that runs separately afterwards.

source.author: Shashank
source.subject: ask: per-declaration vector storage and the opt-in embed pass

pairs.question: Why is the record id a digest of every field and not just content + author + timestamp?

gold.decision_verbatim: The id is a SHA-256 over a domain-tagged, length-prefixed canonical encoding of EVERY field, not only of content + author + timestamp as §4 words it. Those three are the substance of identity — they are what makes two machines agree — but an id that covers only them makes the union LOSSY: two signals with the same text, by the same author, at the same millisecond, anchored to two different symbols collide, and a set keyed on id then holds one id and two payloads with no way out but picking one. Picking one is last-writer-wins wearing a different name, and it is exactly what this contract exists to delete. union_keeps_records_that_share_all_three_substantive_fields is that argument as a test: seven records identical in content, author and timestamp, all seven kept.

pairs.question: Why are record timestamps supplied by the caller instead of captured?

gold.decision_verbatim: Timestamps are supplied by the caller and never captured. A captured timestamp makes an id depend on the machine that built it, so the same event ingested twice on two machines gets two ids and sync becomes a duplicate storm rather than a union; re-ingesting one row is idempotent by construction instead of by an "already seen" table someone has to remember to consult. record.c contains no clock at all — the wall clock is its own translation unit and the contract script asserts the absence, because that failure only surfaces after two machines have both ingested the same feed.

pairs.question: Why does the address wrap the qualified name instead of replacing it?

gold.decision_verbatim:
The qualified name is FORMALISED, not superseded. A canonical name already
exists and is load-bearing in four places — UNIQUE(project, qualified_name) in
store.c, the graph-buffer merge key, the vector table's primary key and the MCP
handle. Superseding it would leave the address and the store's own uniqueness
key disagreeing about what one node is, which is the two-ends divergence this
phase exists to prevent. So the address wraps the qualified name in the two
scopes it does not carry and leaves it byte-for-byte untouched as the terminal
field.

pairs.question: Why is the unescaped dot in a qualified name not fixed?

gold.decision_verbatim:
The unescaped dot is not fixed, deliberately. fqn_compute("proj", ".env.local",
"__file__") is still "proj..env.local.__file__" and a qualified name still
cannot be split back into segments. The ADDRESS is unambiguous anyway, because
it never splits one: slugs are project names, so neither '/' nor '#' can occur
in them, and the leftmost split of each separates the fields exactly with the
qualified name taken verbatim to end of string. Escaping would identify a node
the store cannot look up.

pairs.question: Why does a content match at a different address never re-attach the anchor?

gold.decision_verbatim:
CANDIDATES ARE EVIDENCE, NEVER A DECISION (I5). Cross-directory move, file
rename and copy-paste all produce the identical observation — a different
address whose content hashes the same, HYP_ADDR_REL_CONTENT_ONLY — and this
contract cannot tell them apart, so it does not pretend to. A copy-paste yields
SEVERAL candidates, possibly with the untouched original among them;
re-attaching to one automatically would pin last month's reasoning to code that
never had it. So a hash match at a DIFFERENT QN is never RESOLVED. This unit
GATHERS candidates with their evidence; C4u presents them; nothing re-attaches.
They are sorted by address so presentation is deterministic, and scan_skipped
is published because a candidate list is a FLOOR whenever a span could not be
read or addressed — C4u must disclose that, not absorb it.

pairs.question: Why does the span hash ride in FRONT of the address in an anchor string?

gold.decision_verbatim:
The hash rides in FRONT. The QN is the address's TERMINAL field and may contain
any printable byte, '@' included, so a suffix hash could collide with a QN that
ends in '@' + 32 hex chars — re-opening exactly the ambiguity identity.h closed
by making the QN terminal. A prefix cannot collide: an address always begins
"hyp1:" and 'y' is not a hex digit, so the two grammars are disjoint at byte 1.
A test composes that adversarial QN and round-trips it.

pairs.question: Why does a symbol that slides 200 lines still resolve?

gold.decision_verbatim:
CLASSIFICATION, AS IMPLEMENTED. Symbol identity first, content hash second,
line numbers NEVER — lines are output only, which is why a symbol that slides
200 lines stays RESOLVED with no special case: there was never a line number in
the question. The test asserts exactly that, with start_line visibly moving
1 -> 201 while the classification does not move at all.

  RESOLVED           QN found; no hash recorded, or the recorded hash matches.
  RESOLVED_EDITED    QN found, hash differs. STILL ATTACHED — the QN is the
                     identity; reasoning gone stale is a different problem from
                     reasoning gone lost.
  ORPHANED           QN not found. With a recorded hash, every span in the
                     workspace whose CURRENT content hashes to it becomes a
                     candidate.
  UNKNOWN_WORKSPACE  the address names a workspace matching none known. A
                     visible error NAMING the workspace — never an empty
                     result, which would read as "nothing attached" and is a
                     claim about the wrong universe.
  ERROR (= 0)        could not classify. Deliberately the zero value, so a
                     zeroed struct reads as "no classification happened" and

pairs.question: Why is the decision store an id-keyed set rather than an append-only log?

gold.decision_verbatim:
NOT A LOG, AND WHERE THAT IS ACTUALLY ENFORCED. The obvious implementation is
an append-only log, and it breaks the union: a log has an order, the order is
machine-local, and the moment it means anything two stores holding the same
records stop being the same store. So the on-disk form is an ID-KEYED SET.
`records` is WITHOUT ROWID, which does not merely leave the engine's insertion
counter unused — `SELECT rowid FROM records` does not parse. The column set is
exactly id plus the nine frozen record fields: no sequence, no offset, no
position, no workspace, no store-invented timestamp. Kind is stored by its
stable NAME, so renumbering the enum cannot rewrite anyone's store.

source.author: Shashank
source.subject: store: the decision store is an id-keyed set, and the set type is what makes it one

gold.marker: NOT A LOG, AND WHERE THAT IS ACTUALLY ENFORCED

pairs.question: Why are record vectors keyed on a hash of the content instead of the record id?

pairs.question: Why do record vectors live in a sibling store rather than in ask_vectors' file?

gold.decision_verbatim:
WHY A SIBLING STORE, NOT A TABLE IN ask_vectors' FILE. Same schema family,
different scope. <cache>/vectors/<project>.db is per-project and every claim it
makes — graph_generation, whole_file_spans, prune-by-QN — is a claim about one
project's corpus. Records are global memory: no project, no generation, no
qualified name. Housing them there either duplicates them per project (the N×
again, one level down) or nominates one project's file as "the" memory store.

record vectors must outlive that. And the code-span table is keyed on
qualified_name for documented reasons; one table with two key disciplines needs

pairs.question: Why does the secret scrub run before the record is built rather than after?

gold.decision_verbatim:
WHY THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE UNIT. Transcripts contain pasted keys — the session
that scheduled this one contained two. C2 makes that permanent rather than
merely embarrassing: the id commits to `content`, records are immutable, and
sync is a union, so an unscrubbed record may already be on another machine
before anyone notices. There is no post-hoc scrub. Scrubbing after the build
changes the content, which changes the id, which is a DIFFERENT record — the
original is still there, still syncing. So the scrub runs before construction
and the scrubbed text is what the id binds.

pairs.question: Why does index_status report `missing` rather than `behind`?

gold.decision_verbatim:
`missing`, NEVER `behind`. The record store is an id-keyed set whose canonical
order is content-addressed and deliberately non-semantic (C2). A union has no
total order, so "40 behind" is a number nothing can produce; "40 records the
upstream set holds that I do not" is one that can. Set-digest compare first —
equal digests are equal sets, so the yes/no is free — then an id walk for the
count plus the NAMES, because a bare count is a number nobody can act on. The
list is capped at 64 and the withheld remainder is disclosed; the disclosure
key is ABSENT when nothing was withheld. Records only the LOCAL side holds are
not counted: those are writes a push has not delivered, not staleness here.

source.author: Shashank

pairs.question: Why does a repository's role come from existing registries instead of a list?

gold.decision_verbatim:
WHY THIS IS NOT A LIST. A workspace holds many trees and only some of them are
yours. The cheap way to answer "which" is a hand-written list of vendored
directories — and a list is only as good as its enumeration. Twice in this
project the missed entry was the most user-facing one. So every rule here READS
a registry that already exists somewhere else, and adds no second place to
declare anything:

  - A2 vendored   scripts/vendored-checksums.txt, the same manifest
                  security-vendored.sh verifies and license-gate.sh walks. This
                  module is a fourth reader of it. Newly vendored code becomes
                  role `vendored` the moment the existing gates learn about it,
                  with no edit here.
  - A3 generated  two signals: the tree is gitignored by its enclosing
                  repository (same hyp_gitignore engine discovery uses), or a
                  bounded sample says so — up to 64 files, first 4096 bytes of
                  each, strict majority carrying DO NOT EDIT / @generated.
                  A sample, deliberately: reading every byte of every file to
                  answer a metadata question is the wrong trade, and the
                  derived-do-not-edit token is what keeps the heuristic honest.
  - A4 upstream   THE RULE: normalise the tree's origin remote to a lowercase
                  "owner/name" coordinate (files only, worktree gitdir and
                  commondir indirection followed, no subprocess). Equal to the
                  workspace's own origin → not upstream, that is another
                  checkout of this project. In the known-upstream set → upstream.
                  Anything else → no signal; a random clone is not "upstream of
                  nothing". The set is loaded from audit-license-provenance.py's
                  LIBS/FORKS tables and the grammar MANIFEST.md upstream rows —
                  read, never typed.
  - A5 reference  the only role that cannot be derived, because "I added this
                  repo for inspiration" is intent, not a property of a tree.

source.author: Shashank

pairs.question: Why is the workspace id derived rather than taken from the first repo's slug?

gold.decision_verbatim:
THE ID IS DERIVED, NEVER "THE FIRST REPO'S SLUG". Two machines that name a
workspace differently produce disjoint address spaces, and C6u's union merges
them SILENTLY — the record field set is frozen, so prevention here is the only
fix available. In order: the TOML `name` when present; otherwise, for one
member, that member's own slug (this is what makes the migration an identity);
otherwise "ws-" + 16 hex of SHA-256 over the SORTED member slugs,
domain-tagged and length-prefixed. A pure function of the member SET —
enumeration order, declaration order, and which repo happened to come first
cannot reach it. The stated limitation is in the header rather than papered
over: member slugs are per-path, so the same repos checked out elsewhere derive
a different id, and the remedy is the TOML name.

pairs.question: Why is `origin` in the watched-ingest format a file position?

gold.decision_verbatim:
ORIGIN IS POSITIONAL, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. `wd1:<relpath>@<offset>`.
The same file position re-ingests to the same record id, so re-ingest is
idempotent with no dedup table anywhere (I8). Two byte-identical rows at two
positions stay two records — which is what makes D4's set-of-origins audit a
real comparison instead of a count, because a count cannot tell dedup from
loss. The price is stated in the doc rather than hidden: feed files must be
appended to, never rewritten or truncated. A shrunk file is refused by name and
stays refused for the scanner's lifetime; regrowing it does not restore trust
in offsets already ingested under the old ones.

pairs.question: Why does watched ingest refuse a line that supplies its own origin or id?

gold.decision_verbatim:
THE WRITER SUPPLIES WHAT WAS SAID; THE ADAPTER DERIVES WHERE IT CAME FROM.

pairs.question: Why does the encoder have to report which device actually ran?

gold.decision_verbatim:
The thing that makes a fallback safe is that it is never silent. A run
that asked for a GPU and quietly got a CPU takes fifteen times as long
and produces an identical file, so the only defence is to write down
what happened:

  - the encoder seam gains device_note() and device_is_gpu(), both
    required, and an encoder that will not say gets "UNKNOWN" rather
    than a guessed "CPU" — a wrong device note is worse than an absent
    one because it is believed;
  - `--device auto|gpu|cpu` expresses the REQUEST, device_note reports
    the OUTCOME, and the two are deliberately different fields;
  - the pass logs a warning and the command prints a starred line when
    a GPU was asked for and not used;
  - ask_index gains a device_note column, so `--status` can say what a
    45-minute build and a 3-minute build otherwise cannot be told apart
    by. Not a reuse gate: track 2 measured GPU and CPU vectors agreeing
    at min cosine 0.9996, so mixing devices is safe. Mixing models is
    not, and that is a separate field.

- n_ctx is TOTAL KV capacity and llama.cpp DIVIDES it by n_seq_max, so

    and is not is n_batch * n_seq_max: 8192 x 64 is 524,288 tokens of

    inadmissible on this card, forever.

    configurations exactly (896 / 2,016 / 4,032 / 8,064 / 14,336 MB),

pairs.question: What gates escalation — the prefix contract or something else?

gold.decision_verbatim:
THE GATE IS A SPACE ID, NOT THE PREFIX CONTRACT. A cosine between two models'
vectors means something only if they share an embedding space, and cross-space
failure is SILENT — score a Qwen3 index against a voyage query and nothing
errors, the ranking is ordinary-looking and wrong, the worst failure for a
tool an agent trusts. `hyp_ask_space_id_for_model` (ask_vectors.h, the storage
seam both the embed pass and the ask handler already include) returns
"voyage-4" for the voyage-4 family (nano/large/lite/4, with or without the

"-Q8_0@<revision>") and NULL for EVERYTHING else — voyage-code-3 (same vendor,
one generation back, measured NOT shared: 0.0047 vs 0.005 chance), Qwen3
(0.0034), Jina, Gemini (unmeasured -> refused), "" (not recorded). The
allowlist earns its authority from §2.15's eight negative controls, and is
extended by a measurement, never a model card. The index stamps
`ask_index.space_id` (added defaulted column, the prefix_contract precedent;

at ask time the stamp is used if present, else derived from model_id through

space is unknown or the two differ, naming both model ids and both spaces, and
when the provider's dim_mode is REEMBEDS (a re-embedding head is a different

pairs.question: Why did a warm daemon spend the owner's escalation key?

gold.decision_verbatim:
The read itself is per request — `getenv` runs inside
hyp_ask_provider_encoder_create on every escalated call — but `environ` is a
snapshot taken at exec, so the value it finds belongs to the shell that started
the process doing the reading. In this build that process is always the daemon:
the stdio MCP entry point is a thin frontend to it, `hyponoia cli <tool>`
connects to it, and the graph UI's /api/embed-view/ask runs inside it. So any
local process of this uid that can reach the socket could spend against the
owner's account without ever holding the key.

pairs.question: Why was reading the key from the requesting context rejected?

gold.decision_verbatim:
(a) Read the key from the REQUESTING context. Rejected on its merits, not for
    effort. The client is a third-party MCP host; only hyponoia's own frontend
    sees its environment, and forwarding the VALUE over the socket would put
    the key in a second process's heap and on a wire for the life of a session
    — the exact opposite of ask_provider.h's rule that it is read at the moment
    of use and never stored. Forwarding a HASH instead leaks nothing, and buys
    nothing: against a same-uid threat model where /proc/<daemon>/environ is
    already readable, proof-of-possession stops accidents, not adversaries. It
    would cost a change to the daemon's session-context frame, and would still
    leave the graph UI's HTTP route uncovered, because a browser has no
    environment at all.
(b) Keep the read, make it visible. Necessary and not sufficient: it tells the
    owner what happened and gives them no way to stop it.
(c) Require an opt-in for a shared process to hold a key at all.
(d) (c) with (b) — what this does.

source.author: Shashank
source.subject: keep a warm daemon from spending the owner's escalation key

pairs.question: Why did the MCP server die on a large query_graph reply, and what replaced that?

gold.decision_verbatim:
Root cause is a conflation, not the limit itself. application_mcp_request
checked only response_length > UINT32_MAX and passed anything smaller on, so an
oversized reply reached the transport, which rejected the frame. The frontend
worker cannot tell that rejection from a dead socket, and for a dead socket it
deliberately _Exit()s the process — closing the kernel IPC handle is the only
portable way to cancel daemon session ownership from a thread blocked in stdio.
Correct for a broken transport; a fatal over-reaction to a large answer.

pairs.question: Why does ordinary malloc go through mimalloc on Linux but not on macOS?

gold.decision_verbatim:
macOS stays off deliberately and permanently: enabling the override there
compiles alloc-override.c's forwarding definitions, and under the two-level
namespace this binary's free becomes mi_free while system libraries keep
allocating from the system allocator, so the first pointer crossing that
boundary aborts with "mi_free: invalid pointer". ELF's flat namespace has no
such split, which is why Linux can have this and macOS cannot.

pairs.question: Why are test seams opt-in rather than opt-out?

gold.decision_verbatim:
Test seams are now opt-in, never opt-out. TEST_SEAMS=1 defines
CBM_ENABLE_TEST_SEAMS; without it the crash-orphan probe -- which forks a child
that ignores SIGTERM and loops forever, then writes its pid to a caller-supplied
path -- and the lease-ownership marker compile to trivial stubs, so call sites are
untouched and the binary holds no fork, no signal handler and no env-var string.
Opt-IN is the point: forgetting the flag yields a clean binary rather than a leaky
one. scripts/test.sh requests it in the leg that consumes it, and
tests/test_worker_watchdog.sh now asserts the capability up front instead of
dying later with an opaque "Killed: 9".

pairs.question: Why does the cohort guard key the rendezvous on the cache root?

HYP_DAEMON_RUNTIME_PARENT is the escape a normal build gets, and it keeps the

pairs.question: Why is `sync_memory` not an MCP tool?

gold.decision_verbatim:
- **C6u** [C1u] Sync: push/pull as a **union** of append-only records. Push is "merge my set into
  theirs", pull is the reverse — **no outbox, no pending-write queue**, which would be state that
  can disagree with the store. Offline writes locally and pushes later by the same merge.
  **The trigger is the code index, not an agent and not a clock.** `sync_memory` as an MCP tool is
  **CUT** — its own author named it the cut-first candidate, and the owner's ruling is sharper: sync
  runs **when a repo in the workspace changes locally**, because a changed tree is exactly the
  moment an agent will ask "what happened here" and the relevant memory must already be present.
  The watcher that already re-indexes on change fires the memory pull in the same pass. Push
  follows a local `record_memory`. No agent-callable sync surface; `hyp sync` on the CLI for the
  manual case.

pairs.question: Why can orphan-ness not be stored on the record?

gold.decision_verbatim:
- **C4u** [C3u] **Orphaning, and this is the unit that matters most.** First, a constraint from C2:
  **orphan-ness cannot live ON the record** — the anchor is in the id preimage, so a record cannot
  be marked. It is either **derived at read time** or recorded as a new `signal` pointing back via
  `parent`, and it is a property of *(record, index state)*, so two machines may legitimately
  disagree about it. "Visibly orphaned" means visible in the read path, not a flag. **Any change to
  the qualified name orphans an anchor, and the content hash yields candidates that include
  copies** — cross-dir move, file rename and copy-paste all land in the same
  `CONTENT_ONLY` relation, so the copy-paste case yields TWO candidates and re-attaches to neither.
  A rename orphans an anchor —
  `f95d6841` broke seven things a rename could not see. An orphaned anchor becomes **visibly
  orphaned**: never silently dropped, never silently re-attached to a plausible neighbour. A false
  negative makes a decision unfindable; a false positive attaches last month's reasoning to code
  that never had it, which is worse.
gold.marker: orphan-ness cannot live ON the record
